column1: # Generated messages for the PRODUCTION-SHAPED cluster.
#   topic <TAB> generator <TAB> count <TAB> layout
# `generator` names one of the awk programs in the generate() function in seed.sh; `layout` is the
# same vocabulary the hand-written data files use in their `#mode:` line — value-only, key-value,
# or headers-key-value — and has to match what that generator emits.
# WHY THESE ARE GENERATED AND NOT WRITTEN DOWN
# The hand-written files under data/ exist to be read. Every line in them was written by a person
# for a person to look at: an order that was cancelled, a dead letter whose headers point at a real
# offset in another topic, a log line that is deliberately not JSON. There are only ever a few
# dozen, and that is right — nobody wants to scroll past ten thousand records to find the
# interesting one.
# But a virtualised table, an offset-range seek, a partition filter over twenty-four partitions,
# and a consumer group that is eight thousand messages behind are not exercised by forty records.
# They need volume, and volume must not live in git: twenty thousand JSON documents would be
# roughly six megabytes of repository that nobody will ever read a line of.
# So these are produced at seed time from a fixed random seed derived from the topic name. The
# same topic gets the same messages on every run, on every machine — so a screenshot taken today
# still matches the data next month — and the repository stays small.
# THE COST
# Twenty thousand records is the number where the message browser has real work to do and the seed
# still finishes in seconds. All four topics are produced concurrently, one JVM each, with large
# batches and lz4 compression, so the wall-clock cost is roughly one producer's, not four.
# The firehose. No key, so records land round-robin across all twenty-four partitions and no
# partition is more interesting than another. About one event in five carries an experiment block
# the others do not, because that is what an event stream looks like after a year of shipping.
analytics.pageviews
# Keyed by session, so a partition filter returns one coherent set of visitors rather than a
# shuffle. Twelve partitions and five thousand records: enough that paging matters.
clickstream.raw
# The compacted topic at volume. Four thousand records over about nine hundred keys, so keys
# repeat many times and the log cleaner has genuine work to do, and six per cent of them are
# tombstones — a key with a null value, which is how a delete is written in Kafka. A message
# browser has to draw that as absence, not as an empty string.
search.index-updates
# Per-minute service metrics over the last day. One value in forty is a latency in the seconds
# rather than the milliseconds, so there is something findable when you type a filter.
platform.metrics
